item.title: Affective representations and brain-body dynamics during emotional video viewing
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Emotional events evoke changing neural and bodily responses, but how these responses relate to overall emotional evaluations and how brain and body responses correspond over time remain unclear. Ninety-two participants viewed 25 silent emotional videos, each approximately one minute long, and rated valence and arousal after each video. We recorded brain activity using magnetoencephalography alongside cardiac, electrodermal, respiratory and facial-muscle activity. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) compared source-resolved cortical spectral patterns and peripheral response patterns with participants' valence and arousal ratings, adjusting each affective dimension for the other. Across whole videos, valence similarity corresponded to beta-band power patterns predominantly in left sensorimotor and frontotemporal cortex and to facial-muscle responses. Arousal similarity corresponded to alpha-band power patterns in the right frontoparietal cortex and to phasic electrodermal activity. The neural associations persisted after adjustment for visual and semantic similarities between the videos. Windowed neural correspondence with retrospective valence was significant from around 10 s onwards, with both neural and facial-muscle associations strengthening towards the end of the videos, whereas no significant windowed arousal associations were detected throughout viewing. We further applied dynamic RSA to compare neural and physiological response patterns across videos at different temporal lags. Correspondence exceeded a temporally decoupled reference for facial muscles, heart rate and electrodermal activity, but not respiration rate. On average, corrugator activity preceded corresponding neural patterns by about 1 s, zygomaticus activity occurred at approximately the same time, and heart-rate and electrodermal activity followed about 1.7 s and 4.5 s later, respectively. Together, these findings link overall affective evaluations to complementary neural and peripheral response geometries and reveal signal-specific temporal profiles of ongoing brain-body correspondence.

item.title: In Utero MRI of Radial Glial Fibers Highlights Their Role in Modulating Fetal Cortical Folding
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The process of cortical folding is fundamental to early human brain development. While the differential growth of the cortical layers is a known driver, the biomechanical contribution of key cellular microstructures remains unclear, and there is a lack of direct in vivo markers of cortical microstructures for time-resolved observations. Using a multimodal approach combining in utero and ex vivo fetal brain MRI, histology, and computational mechanical simulation, we investigated whether developmental reorganization of cortical radial microstructures, particularly the radial glial cell (RGC)-associated scaffold, is linked to cortical folding and may modulate its mechanical progression. We characterized this radial organization noninvasively using diffusion MRI-based radial fiber density ( FD rad ). ex vivo fetal brain MRI and histology supported that regional variations in FD rad were strongly associated with vimentin-labelled radial architecture. Our in utero MRI data revealed closely coordinated developmental changes in cortical FD rad and curvature, with their regional timings and spatial patterns significantly coupled across the cortex. Longitudinal in utero MRI data further supported the synchronized within-individual co-development of FD rad and curvature. Furthermore, biomechanical simulations showed that reducing radial reinforcement modulated differential-growth-driven buckling, producing earlier folding and a greater cortical curvature under otherwise matched model conditions. Collectively, this study introduces FD rad as a noninvasive in utero MRI measure sensitive to radial glial fibers. By integrating spatial, temporal, histological, and computational evidence, our findings suggested a model in which developmental disassembly of the radial scaffold may modulate the mechanical response of the fetal cortex to differential growth, thereby contributing to cortical folding.

item.title: The Aging Brain Matrix: Cross-Species Evidence Linking FREM3 to Brain and Cognitive Aging
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The human extracellular-matrix-related FREM3 gene is strongly age-dependent, enriched in age-sensitive excitatory long-range-projecting neurons, and implicated in neurodegenerative diseases. To establish the first translationally relevant causal evidence for the gene’s roles in brain structure and cognition, we developed an excitatory-neuron-specific Frem3 conditional knockout mouse model ( Frem3 -cKO) and computed genetically regulated expression of FREM3 ( FREM3 -GReX) in humans, enabling convergent neurostructural and cognitive characterizations. Frem3 -cKO mice showed widespread lower global and regional brain volume in middle age vs young adulthood, consistent with drastic age-dependent volume loss absent in wildtype mice. These effects were strongest in cognitively relevant cortical regions and paralleled by lower cognitive performance. In humans, lower FREM3- GReX was associated with lower total surface area, which further mediated an indirect link to lower cognitive performance across multiple age-sensitive domains. We provide the first translationally relevant cross-species evidence supporting a key role for FREM3/Frem3 in maintaining brain and cognitive health across aging.

item.title: A Wasserstein Weisfeiler-Lehman Kernel Framework for Multimodal Brain Connectome Analysis
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract We introduce a Wasserstein Weisfeiler-Lehman (WWL) graph-kernel framework for the joint analysis of weighted structural graphs and continuous node attributes, together with a regularized fractional-Laplacian extension of the underlying graph propagation operator. The proposed fractional operator provides non-local propagation across the entire graph, with influence decaying as a power law with graph distance, while remaining anchored to the subject-specific structural topology. This extends the standard finite-range Weisfeiler Lehman propagation scheme to a controlled long-range setting without introducing an externally prescribed coupling between structural and functional information. We formulate the framework for multimodal brain connectivity by representing each subject as a single attributed graph: diffusion tractography defines the weighted structural edges, while resting-state functional connectivity profiles are encoded as continuous node attributes. We evaluate the method on a synthetic cohort of $900$ subjects in three ordered clinical groups along the Alzheimer's disease spectrum, generated from multiple structural templates and characterised by a spatially structured loss of resting-state network segregation with age. Under nested cross-validation, the WWL kernel achieves a balanced accuracy of $0.651\pm0.028$, significantly outperforming both a raw-feature SVM and a histogram-based WL-kernel baseline. Controlled ablations separate the contribution of the Wasserstein representation from that of structural propagation. Replacing the propagation operator by the identity yields essentially identical classification performance, whereas a structure-only representation approaches chance, showing that the discriminative gain in this benchmark is primarily associated with the Wasserstein point-cloud representation rather than structural propagation. Conversely, experiments across distinct signal regimes show that the fractional extension is signal-dependent: non-local propagation can improve continuous prediction for diffuse whole-brain coupling signals, but provides no consistent advantage for network-segregation signals. We further identify a connectivity artefact induced by fixed-percentile structural sparsification and establish a threshold preserving graph connectivity across subjects. The results clarify the respective roles of Wasserstein geometry, structural propagation, and non-locality in multimodal graph representations and provide a controlled framework for assessing when fractional graph propagation is expected to be beneficial.

item.title: Hexagonal modulation of theta rhythmic attentional sampling of visual space.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Spatial attention improves visual perception by selecting behaviorally relevant sensory signals. Traditionally, attention has been conceptualized as a static spotlight, while recent evidence posited that attention operates as a moving spotlight that samples visual space sequentially in discrete snapshots that are clocked by theta rhythms (∼3-8 Hz). While theta rhythmic attentional sampling has mainly been observed in fronto-parietal and occipital areas, theta oscillations also hallmark entorhinal-hippocampal grid-cell networks, which encode physical space in hexagonal patterns that guide overt exploration and navigation. We hypothesized that visual attention might rely on the same underlying principles and sample visual space in a hexagonal, grid-like configuration. To test this hypothesis, twenty participants (10 females and 10 males) performed a cue-guided attention task that probed behavioral performance as a function of space and time. Reaction times were assessed as a function of spatial location and varying cue-target intervals, which displayed spatially-structured theta rhythms. Specifically, higher theta power occurred at spatial locations that were aligned to multiples of 60°, consistent with an underlying hexagonal organization. Participants that exhibited stronger hexagonal sampling relied less on the spatial cue to guide their attentional allocation. In sum, these findings suggest that covert visual attention is organized in a hexagonal pattern that might be consistent with the grid-like structure known from the entorhinal-hippocampal system and highlight that theta rhythms could reflect a common organizing principle for spatial cognition.Significance Statement Attention prioritizes sensory inputs to optimize behavior. But how does attention sample the environment in space and time? Here, we demonstrate that attentional sampling of visual space is not uniform, but might preferentially explore locations that are oriented along a hexagonal pattern, reminiscent of the spatial configuration of entorhinal-hippocampal grid cells. Moreover, covert attentional sampling exhibited oscillatory theta signatures (3-8 Hz). In sum, these findings suggest that spatial attention and navigation may share a common organizing principle, and indicate that theta rhythms may orchestrate sampling behaviors in space and time as a unifying principle underlying spatial cognition.

item.title: Perception of tones versus tone streams under random multi-tone masking and its representation in auditory cortex.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
When repeated tones are presented among random masker tones, their perceptual organization is often variable. In some trials, they cannot be segregated from the masker tones. In other trials, often with a delay, they form coherent streams, segregated from the masker tones. A strong awareness-related negativity is evoked by each segregated tone of the stream in auditory cortex. A similar negative-going response has been observed when subtle, isolated tones are detected versus missed, raising the question of whether target tones that do not form a stream under informational masking are still perceived or not. Here a paradigm is introduced to probe this question while activity in auditory cortex was recorded with magnetoencephalography. Human listeners (13 female, 8 male) were instructed to indicate when they detected an isochronous stream of tones under multi-tone masking while listening to the stimulus. Thereafter, they indicated if a cue tone, presented subsequently to each trial, was comprised in the target and masker combination. Results confirmed that target tones could still be perceived in the subset of trials where they did not form a coherent stream, but the detectability in the cued frequency report was higher for tones forming a stream. A prominent awareness-related negativity was only observed when the tones formed a stream, suggesting that this response reflects the perceptual organization of the tones into streams and beyond the pure perception of the tones themselves. We speculate that the perceptual organization into a stream further enhances the detectability of the tones comprised in the stream.Significance Statement Tone sequences may form streams that segregate from competing aspects of the auditory scene, a phenomenon considered comparable to visual object grouping. In multi-tone masking, hearing out streams of repeated tones seemingly enhances tone detectability by a degree that makes it difficult to judge whether these tones could at all be perceived if they had not formed a coherent stream. We present a paradigm that allows for probing both, the perception of target-tone frequency and the formation of coherent streams in the same trials. Applying this setup in magnetoencephalography showed that the perceptual organization into a stream is more strongly represented in auditory cortex than the ability to correctly detect a tone frequency within a random tone masker.

item.title: Bivalent habenula modulation of human monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The habenula is implicated in signaling negative reward prediction errors (RPE), yet direct evidence demonstrating its influence on downstream human brain circuits is limited. Using ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and dynamic causal modelling across two negative RPE-inducing experimental tasks, we characterize habenula-directed connectivity with monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways in healthy adults (n = 47, 24 males and 23 females; n = 43, 23 males and 20 females). Negative feedback drove habenula inhibition of ventral tegmental area and dorsal raphe nucleus activity, while positive feedback had an excitatory effect. These core effects are replicated across reversal learning and perceptual decision uncertainty tasks, establishing a generalizable mechanism for behavioral adaptation. Task-specific modulatory effects emerged in pathways between the subcortical and cortical regions (ventral tegmental area→dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, dorsal raphe nucleus→medial prefrontal cortex, and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex→habenula), revealing context-dependent cortical elaboration of negative RPE-driven habenula signals. This provides the first evidence in humans, using model-based effective connectivity, for bivalent modulation of habenula function on monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways, demonstrating how the brain integrates negative and positive signals to guide adaptive behavior.Significance Statement The habenula - an epithalamic brain region - plays a key role in the encoding of reward and punishment. Animal studies have demonstrated the habenula to be bivalently modulated by aversive and appetitive stimuli, resulting in the bidirectional modulation of monoaminergic brain region activity. Despite this evidence, the directional impact of bivalently modulated habenula activity on its circuitry has yet to be investigated in humans. This study leverages ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and dynamic causal modelling to reveal the impact of bivalent habenula modulation on monoaminergic midbrain and cortical regions across two distinct tasks. Through these methodologies, we demonstrate the habenula to have a key role in guiding adaptive behavior.

item.title: Intrinsic gestational timing governs human cerebellar development after preterm birth.
item.description:
Science (New York, N.Y.)
Intrinsic programs shape brain maturation; however, which of these programs are perturbed by prematurity as well as the molecular pathways involved remain unknown. The human cerebellum serves as a paradigm of extrauterine development-its accelerated growth and circuit formation align with the third trimester, a period disrupted by preterm delivery. Using multimodal datasets encompassing in vivo neuroimaging and neurodevelopmental outcomes with postmortem spatial-transcriptomic and histopathological profiling, we show that prematurity diverts the cerebellar developmental trajectory. Cerebellar growth and functional outcomes scaled with gestational age, despite modifying perinatal exposures. Spatially resolved developmental programs underlying macroscopic trajectories were marked by incomplete granule cell maturation and impaired Purkinje cell structural refinement, which indicate lineage-specific developmental asynchrony. Thus, prematurity constitutes biologically displaced maturation, in which infants of equivalent postmenstrual age occupy divergent developmental states.

item.title: The amygdaloid complex: from morphology to neurodegeneration.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
The amygdaloid complex is one of the most structurally and functionally heterogeneous regions of the mammalian brain, acting as an integrative node between sensory, mnemonic and visceral systems. It comprises a set of subnuclei whose cytoarchitectural differentiation, neurochemical profiles and anatomical boundaries have been debated since the earliest descriptions. This heterogeneity is established during ontogenetic development, assembling progenitors from pallial and subpallial domains, and preoptic and hypothalamic territories, resulting in a highly connected network. Maturation is not complete at birth, the amygdala changes through childhood and adolescence, leaving a protracted window of environmental sensitivity. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics have added a molecular layer to this framework, resolving populations that no single marker separates, and set explicit limits on the resolution at which rodent-derived subdivisions can be transferred to the human amygdala. Together these levels of description provide a structural framework for understanding its functions, which include emotional regulation and conditioned fear, social and sexual behaviours, decision-making, reward and punishment processing, empathy and memory modulation. Cross-species comparison reveals further variation, particularly the expansion of the basolateral complex in primates and the redistribution of neurons towards the lateral nucleus in humans. In summary, the amygdala acts as a densely connected hub with a broad role not only in physiological and psychological health but also in disease states; indeed, the amygdala is affected early in several neurodegenerative disorders, and in some (notably limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy and argyrophilic grain disease) it is among the first regions in which pathology is detected.

item.title: Cerebellar subregions support social cognition in early behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Social cognitive deficits manifest early in behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), compromising individuals' ability to interpret social cues, empathize, and maintain interpersonal relationships. Current neurobiological models emphasize cortical network disruption, particularly within the salience, semantic appraisal, and default mode networks, as primary contributors to social dysfunction. However, despite the increasingly recognized role of the cerebellum in higher-order cognitive and socioemotional processes, its contributions to social deficits remains underexplored in bvFTD. Here, we investigated the unique and network-level influences of cerebellar subregions on social cognition across experimental and real-world assessments in early-stage bvFTD. A total of 107 individuals with bvFTD and 100 healthy controls were evaluated across three social domains: theory of mind (ToM) (The Awareness of Social Inference Test-Social Inference-Enriched, TASIT-SIE; Cognitive Emotional Perspective Taking Test), emotion reading (Dynamic Affect Recognition Test; TASIT-Emotion Evaluation Test; Comprehensive Affect Testing System), and real-life empathy (Revised Self-Monitoring Scale; Interpersonal Reactivity Index). Using a functional cerebellar parcellation, we extracted volumes of posterior cerebellar subregions implicated in social-linguistic and multiple-demand networks from participants' structural MRIs. To address the high collinearity between cerebellar and cortical atrophy patterns, we applied sequential regression, partial least squares correlation, and dominance analysis to characterize brain-behavior relationships. Additionally, supplementary structural equation modelling (SEM) examined whether the associations between cerebellar integrity and social cognition was mediated by executive functioning. Our results showed that cerebellar subregional integrity contributed to social cognitive deficits in individuals with early-stage bvFTD. Cerebellar subregions, particularly right Crus I and II, showed the strongest and most selective contribution to high-level inferential Theory of Mind performance. Tasks involving dynamic emotion stimuli exhibited a more distributed pattern of cerebello-cerebral involvement. By contrast, questionnaire-based measures of real-world social functioning were less prominently represented in the latent covariance structure. SEM further showed that cerebellar integrity remained directly associated with social cognition after accounting for executive functioning, whereas the indirect association through executive functioning was not significant. These findings highlight the task-dependent nature of cerebellar involvement in social cognition, and demonstrate that time-limited experimental tasks, particularly those involving inferential reasoning about beliefs and affect, are likely to be especially valuable in detecting subtle cerebello-cerebral network dysfunction that questionnaire-based measures may overlook. Our results extend cortex-centric models of social dysfunction in bvFTD by demonstrating that cerebellar subregions contribute to distributed cerebello-cerebral systems associated with social cognitive performance. These findings provide a foundation for future longitudinal and mechanistic studies of cerebello-cerebral dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease.

item.title: Characterizing Narrative Discourse in Posttraumatic Amnesia and Early Recovery After Severe Traumatic Brain Injury.
item.description:
American journal of speech-language pathology
Following severe traumatic brain injury (TBI), individuals experience a transient period of confusion known as posttraumatic amnesia (PTA). Few empirical speech-language pathology studies have described language and cognitive-communication features during PTA or examined their early recovery. International guidelines recommend routine monitoring of communication during PTA; however, standardized speech-language pathology assessments are generally unsuitable for use during PTA. Narrative tasks offer a structured and repeatable approach to capture clinically meaningful changes. The purpose of this research was to describe narrative discourse characteristics in adults with severe TBI during PTA and examine how performance changed following PTA resolution. Nine adults with severe TBI admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation setting completed a narrative task during PTA and again after resolution of PTA. Language samples were analyzed across multiple levels, with descriptive analyses used to characterize performance and patterns of change. Discourse performance during PTA was compared descriptively to published data, providing reference data for microlinguistic measures and story grammar in adults without brain injury and adults with TBI who were not in PTA, where data were available. All participants demonstrated confused, disorganized narratives during PTA, although the degree and profile of impairment varied markedly across individuals. Macrostructural analyses provided the most meaningful and sensitive indicators of change, with several participants showing clearer narrative structure and increased production of relevant content post-PTA. A narrative task has the potential to provide insight into the communication ability of patients in PTA, particularly in relation to change over time. This may help to guide decisions about the most appropriate timing for formal speech-language pathology assessment and intervention.

item.title: Peripersonal space: a neural system mapping self-environment interaction 'here and now'.
item.description:
Trends in cognitive sciences
The space surrounding the body where physical interactions with external stimuli occur is referred to as peripersonal space (PPS). Traditionally conceived as a spatial construct, PPS is better understood as a neural representation that integrates bodily inputs with external cues to predict body-object interactions. After summarizing its multisensory, motor, and plastic properties, this review draws on computational models to examine how PPS captures statistical regularities of body-object interactions. This predictive function may position PPS as an interface between self and environment, contributing to minimal self-consciousness and its alterations across states of consciousness and neuropsychiatric conditions. Recent findings extend this framework to the inner body, suggesting that interoceptive signals shape PPS and that PPS-related processing may influence immune responses.

item.title: Characteristic of anterior cingulate cortex connectivity at subregional level in major depressive disorder.
item.description:
Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology & biological psychiatry
The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) exhibits substantial role underlying the pathophysiology of major depressive disorder (MDD), yet its exact connectivity alteration and the relationship with clinical symptoms remain unclarified. We aimed to systematically investigate ACC subregional functional connectivity alterations with a relatively large sample of MDD and their longitudinal changes associated with clinical state. From the Huaxi Depression Imaging Cohort Study, we recruited 141 MDD patients and 138 matched healthy controls (HC) with complete clinical information and resting-state functional MRI data, and calculated functional connectivity (FC) of five ACC subregions (subgenual, perigenual, rostral, dorsal, and caudal ACC). A subset of patients who completed follow-up clinical assessments and MRI scanning was further classified into remitted and non-remitted subgroups. ACC subregional FC was compared between MDD and HC, and for longitudinal changes in remitted and non-remitted patients separately. Exploratory correlations between FC alterations and symptom profiles were also assessed. Compared with HCs, MDD patients demonstrated widespread hyperconnectivity between most ACC subregions and regions within frontoparietal network (FPN) and default mode network (DMN) at baseline. At follow-up, remitted patients showed reduced connectivity between perigenual ACC (pgACC) and dorsolateral/ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC/vlPFC), with connectivity approaching HC levels. Non-remitted patients, however, exhibited no significant changes. Our findings delineate specific dysconnectivity patterns of ACC at the subregional level in MDD and suggest the pgACC-dlPFC/vlPFC connectivity may represent a candidate neuroimaging correlate of remission.

item.title: Altered stability of dynamic functional architecture in the co-occurrence of autism spectrum disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) frequently co-occur, whereas the underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain largely unexplored. This study aimed to identify alterations in dynamic functional architecture across ASD, ADHD, and their comorbidity. This study selected 287 participants from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange and ADHD-200 datasets, divided into ASD without ADHD (ASD-only), ADHD without ASD (ADHD-only), ASD + ADHD, and typically developing (TD) groups. In this study, we employed dynamic functional stability at the voxel level by measuring the temporal concordance of dynamic functional connectivity (DFC). Furthermore, whole-brain DFC analyses were conducted using clusters with significant stability alterations as seed regions. Group comparisons and correlation analyses were subsequently performed. Our results showed significant group differences in functional stability in the left superior frontal gyrus, orbital part (ORBsup), right pallidum, and left amygdala. Seed-based analyses identified altered DFC variability between the left amygdala and three regions, including the right middle temporal gyrus (MTG), the left insula, and the left superior occipital gyrus (SOG). Notably, DFC variability between the left amygdala and right MTG was significantly negatively correlated with Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ) scores in the comorbidity group (r = - 0.620, p < 0.01, FDR corrected). From a dynamic perspective, our findings revealed that ASD, ADHD, and their comorbidity exhibited commonanduniquechanges in brain function, thereby enhancing our understanding of the pathogenesis underlying ASD + ADHD.

item.title: Does Phubbing Always Elicit Social Pain? The Role of Belonging Context.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Phubbing, a prevalent interpersonal phenomenon in which individuals divert their attention to their phones while neglecting their interaction partners during face-to-face interactions, has been associated with adverse psychological and relational outcomes, including social pain. However, the same "eyes-on-phone" behavior may not always be experienced as phubbing or evoke feelings of neglect and social pain. The present research examined whether belonging context shapes behavioral and neural responses to "eyes-on-phone" behavior during face-to-face interaction. In Study 1, 163 participants completed a scenario-based task that required them to judge how they felt about several stories, in which belonging context (positive, negative, unrelated) was crossed with attentional state (eyes-on-phone, eyes-on-you). In Study 2, 50 participants completed the Cyberball paradigm to manipulate different belonging contexts (positive, negative, unrelated) with 6 models, followed by an ERP experiment in which they judged whether images of these models displaying different attentional states (eyes-on-phone, eyes-on-you) made them feel neglect-related social pain. Across both studies, within "positive" contexts, "eyes-on-phone" behavior elicited greater social pain, including perceived neglect, emotional unpleasantness, and unwillingness to communicate (Study 1), as well as a greater tendency to endorse neglect-related social pain and larger P3 amplitudes (Study 2) than "eyes-on-you" behavior, whereas this pattern was not consistently observed in the "negative" or "unrelated" contexts. These findings indicate that phubbing is not inherently experienced as social pain. Rather, its social meaning depends on prior belonging context: a mismatch between contextual cues and subsequent attentional behavior may give rise to expectancy violations, which could contribute to social pain when the behavior is interpreted as neglectful.

item.title: Learning Dynamic Affinity Diffusion for Multi-Contrast MRI Super-Resolution via Implicit Neural Representations.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) super-resolution (SR) focuses on reconstructing high-quality, high-resolution target images from sparsely acquired signals while enhancing reconstruction performance through guidance from a reference image. In clinical practice, MRI SR contributes to reduced scan durations and alleviates patient discomfort, as well as motion artifacts associated with extended immobility. Existing SR approaches, however, exhibit insufficient interaction with texture features from the reference image, which results in pronounced inaccuracies at image edges. In addition, these methods often neglect the issue of noise amplification introduced during the SR process. To overcome these limitations, an implicit dynamic spatial propagation network (IDSPN) is introduced, integrating an implicit neural network with dynamic spatial propagation. Initially, residual dense blocks and residual channel attention networks are employed to extract features from the low-resolution input and reference images, respectively. Subsequently, a texture transformer performs feature alignment between the input and reference images and transfers texture information from the reference image to the low-resolution input, followed by upsampling through an implicit neural network. A backbone network then estimates affinity and propagation offsets, enabling refinement via multi-stage iterative diffusion. The proposed approach is evaluated on three publicly available datasets, with experimental findings demonstrating state-of-the-art performance and indicating its potential for clinical application. Codes are available from https://github.com/whj-proj/IDSPN.git.

item.title: Cross-metric convergence reveals altered white matter microstructural-functional correspondence in bipolar ii disorder.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
White matter (WM) microstructural abnormalities are increasingly recognized in bipolar II disorder (BD-II), but it remains unclear how tract-wise microstructural organization corresponds to WM functional connectivity. Diffusion MRI and resting-state fMRI data were acquired from 86 patients with BD-II and 84 healthy controls (HCs). Microstructural profile similarity (MPS) and functional connectivity (FC) matrices were constructed across 48 WM tracts. Following participant-wise, modality-specific standardization of the MPS and FC matrices, tract-wise correspondence was quantified using Spearman correlation and Euclidean profile distance, with self-connections excluded. Group differences were assessed using covariate-adjusted linear models with false discovery rate correction. Sensitivity analyses assessed robustness to clinical sample restrictions and methodological choices. BD-II showed altered MPS-FC correspondence in a restricted set of WM tracts, with 4 tracts identified by Spearman correlation and 6 by Euclidean distance. The left posterior corona radiata (PCR_L) and left external capsule (EC_L) showed convergent abnormalities across both metrics, characterized by higher rank-order correspondence and lower profile distance in BD-II. These convergent findings were stable across several sensitivity analyses but were sensitive to the diffusion-feature normalization reference and Euclidean profile scaling. Neither tract was significantly associated with symptom severity after multiple-comparison correction, whereas exploratory analyses implicated the left uncinate fasciculus in depressive symptom variation. BD-II is associated with altered correspondence between WM microstructural and functional organization. These findings provide multimodal evidence for atypical WM organization and extend current understanding of the neurobiological alterations associated with BD-II.

item.title: Altered centrality and connectivity in motor networks following Xingnao Kaiqiao acupuncture for acute ischemic stroke: a randomized controlled, exploratory fMRI study.
item.description:
Medical & biological engineering & computing
Xingnao Kaiqiao (XNKQ) acupuncture is recommended as an adjunctive intervention for motor dysfunction after acute ischemic stroke (AIS), yet its neuroplastic mechanisms remain unclear. In this randomized, exploratory study, 28 AIS patients were randomly assigned to XNKQ acupuncture plus medication (n = 14) or medication-only (n = 14) to receive 10 sessions of treatment over 14 days. Clinical assessments and resting-state fMRI scanning were conducted before and after the intervention, with brain reorganization analyzed using voxel-wise degree centrality (DC) and seed-based functional connectivity (FC). We found that better recovery in the XNKQ group, reflected by more improvements in NIHSS, total and upper-extremity FMA scores, was correlated with reduced DC in the ipsilesional primary motor cortex (iM1) concurrent with attenuated FC to the contralesional supplementary motor area (cSMA), alongside increased DC in the bilateral SMA and preserved FC between SMA and cerebellar regions. Further exploratory mediation analysis suggested that change in iM1-cSMA FC potentially mediated the relationship between iM1 DC normalization and motor recovery. These preliminary findings suggest that XNKQ acupuncture may facilitate early motor recovery after AIS through normalization of ipsilesional M1 hub centrality and modulation of M1-SMA cross-hemispheric connectivity, providing candidate network markers for acupuncture-associated neuroplasticity.

item.title: Prefrontal circuitry abnormalities and cognitive impairment in adolescents with early-onset psychosis.
item.description:
European child & adolescent psychiatry
Early-onset psychosis (EOP) is associated with marked cognitive impairment and poorer health-related and psychosocial outcomes compared to adult-onset illness, yet the neural mechanisms underlying these deficits during adolescence remain incompletely understood. Despite evidence implicating dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) dysfunction, the region's functional and structural correlates in youth with EOP are not well characterized. Adolescents with EOP (N=31) and healthy controls (HC; N=20) completed NIH Toolbox cognitive assessments and PROMIS self-reports. Prefrontal function was assessed using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) during a Stroop task and at rest. Multimodal MRI, including resting-state fMRI, diffusion tensor imaging, and structural imaging, was used to examine connectivity and morphology of prefrontal and fronto-cerebellar circuits. Adolescents with EOP exhibited poorer cognitive performance across executive functioning domains compared to HC. fNIRS revealed reduced right dlPFC activation on a cognitive control paradigm (p=0.007, pfdr=0.04) and a trend of increased resting-state connectivity between right dlPFC and ventrolateral PFC (p=0.02, pfdr=0.9). Furthermore, resting-state fMRI showed increased dlPFC-striatal connectivity with striatal regions and reduced connectivity with cerebellar Crus I/II (p-FDR<0.05). White matter integrity of the superior longitudinal fasciculus correlated with dlPFC activation during task performance. Structural analyses identified reduced frontal cortical thickness and decreased cerebellar Crus II volumes (p-FWE<0.05) in patients with EOP, with frontal morphology associating with cognitive measures. Cognitive impairment in adolescents with EOP is associated with convergent abnormalities in dlPFC function, fronto-striatal connectivity, and fronto-cerebellar structure. These findings provide preliminary support for a model of disrupted prefrontal circuitry in EOP and highlight the potential clinical value of multimodal imaging markers.

item.title: Early ERP processing of self-referential language processing in voluntary and involuntary action contexts: N170 and EPN.
item.description:
Psychological research
Understanding how the brain differentiates self from others through language represents an important topic in psychology, linguistics, and social cognition. Within an embodied cognition framework, the present EEG study investigated early neural responses to isolated German pronouns varying in self-relatedness (self-, other-, and self/other-related) and grammatical type (personal vs. possessive). Forty right-handed native German speakers silently read visually presented pronouns while EEG activity was recorded. Two task contexts were employed, involving voluntary and involuntary keypress responses following stimulus presentation. Event-related potential (ERP) analyses revealed significant modulations of the N170 and Early Posterior Negativity (EPN) components. N170 amplitudes varied as a function of pronoun type and self-relatedness, with self-related and other-related pronouns eliciting different responses from ambiguous second-person forms. EPN amplitudes differed across self-reference categories, with additional interactions involving hemisphere and pronoun type. Together, these findings suggest that even minimal linguistic stimuli such as pronouns engage early neural processes sensitive to self-relatedness and linguistic context. Task conditions also differed in early ERP amplitudes; because responses in the immediate-response condition overlapped the ERP measurement intervals, these differences are reported without functional attribution.

item.title: Gel-Free Capture of Microvolt-Level Neural Signatures Via a 3D Monolithic Carbon Fiber Dry Electrode.
item.description:
Advanced science (Weinheim, Baden-Wurttemberg, Germany)
Gel-based wet electrodes remain the gold standard for electrophysiology, but gel dehydration limits recordings. Existing dry electrodes partially address this limitation but suffer from high interfacial impedance. Here, a carbon fiber-based porous electrode (CFPE) is reported, comprising a three-dimensional conductive network coated with poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrene sulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS). The CFPE establishes contact at hairy-scalp sites with an impedance of approximately 10 kΩ·cm2. On the forearm, its impedance at 10 Hz without skin preparation is 11.09 ± 1.03 kΩ·cm2, compared with 13.57 ± 2.07 kΩ·cm2 for wet electrodes. After 6 h of wear, CFPE impedance reaches 1.3 times its initial value without skin preparation or gel, whereas wet-electrode impedance reaches 56 times its initial value when applied with skin preparation and conductive gel. High-fidelity electrocardiography, electromyography, and electroencephalography signals are captured with correlation coefficients exceeding 90% and signal-to-noise ratios comparable to wet electrodes. The CFPE further resolves microvolt-level speech-evoked frequency-following responses (FFR) and long-latency responses (LLR), with fidelity comparable to wet electrodes and significantly higher LLR SNR. These results demonstrate gel-free acquisition of weak neural biomarkers, opening a pathway toward prolonged, preparation-free neurophysiology.

item.title: Loose coupling between Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels and release sensors as a synaptic correlate of higher-order brain function.
item.description:
eLife
In the mature neocortex, functionally distinct areas are built by the same archetypes of neurons, but depending on the area, these neurons and their synapses are engaged in very different functions, ranging from lower-order processing of sensory information to higher-order associations and cognitive functions. We found significant differences in the functional presynaptic nanoarchitectures of the same types of pyramidal neuron synapses, depending on whether they are located in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) or in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) of mice. Mature synapses in PFC operated with loose microdomain coupling, as opposed to tight nanodomain coupling in S1. These differences were associated with significant differences in synaptic timing, efficacy, and plasticity between areas. Our data suggest that the mature neocortex uses tuning of synaptic topographies to specialize seemingly identical types of neurons for their required function. They suggest that microdomain coupling in pyramidal neuron synapses could be a presynaptic structure-function correlate of higher-order neocortical functions.

item.title: Ultrasound neuromodulation hypotheses on the directionality of effects and community resource.
item.description:
eLife
Low-intensity transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) is a promising non-invasive technique for brain stimulation and focal neuromodulation. Research with humans and animal models has raised the possibility that TUS can be biased towards enhancing or suppressing neural function. Here, we first collate a set of hypotheses on the directionality of TUS effects and conduct an initial meta-analysis on available healthy human participant TUS studies reporting stimulation parameters and outcomes (n= 47 studies, 52 experiments). In initial exploratory analyses with univariate tests, we find that parameters, such as the intensity and continuity of stimulation (duty cycle, DC) show statistical trends towards likely TUS neural enhancement or suppression of function. Machine-learning analyses were limited by the currently small sample size. Given that human TUS sample sizes are expected to increase, predictability on the directionality of TUS effects could improve if a database is available. Therefore, we establish an inTUS database and resource for the systematic reporting of TUS parameters and outcomes to assist in greater precision in TUS use for brain stimulation and neuromodulation. The paper concludes with a selective review of human clinical TUS studies illustrating how hypotheses on the directionality of TUS effects could be developed for empirical testing in the intended clinical application, not limited to the examples provided.

item.title: The interplay between cortical tracking and functional connectivity in musicians and non-musicians listening to speech and music
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Musical expertise is associated with auditory processing advantages which can extend to the speech domain. However, the origins of such domain-general benefits remain unclear. Recent frameworks propose that better rhythm processing in musicians might be at the basis of the observed advantages in processing music and speech. Auditory cortical tracking and inter-regional interactions between auditory and motor areas have been proposed as key neural mechanisms. In this study, we asked whether expertise-related increase in cortical tracking would be elicited by naturalistic stimuli in clear listening conditions, and whether such effects would be related to audiomotor functional connectivity and individual rhythmic abilities. We compared MEG data from expert musicians and controls with no musical playing experience while they listened to two-minutes long stories and excerpts of piano music. We also collected behavioral data in a rhythmic task testing speech (syllable) production. We found that musicians showed enhanced tracking and enhanced functional connectivity in both speech and music conditions, as well as better rhythmic abilities relative to non-musicians. Alpha connectivity between the right auditory cortex and inferior frontal gyrus negatively predicted cortical tracking across all participants in the speech condition, while no relation was observed for music. We suggest that stronger cortical tracking in musicians is due to domain-general differences in auditory sensory processes and is not driven by motor influences in our experiment. Moreover, a trade-off between cortical tracking and inter-regional communication might be at the basis of optimal perception of speech in both musicians and non-musicians in clear listening conditions.

item.title: Claustrum Morphometry Reveals Spatially Heterogeneous Alterations in 22q11DS
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The human claustrum is a small, irregular, and complexly positioned structure, yet it carries long range projections to most cortical regions responsible for executive functioning. Prior structural MRI research has largely relied on global volume as the metric of its morphology. Such measures may obscure regionally specific morphological changes relevant to developmental and pathological variation. We therefore addressed this limitation by applying longitudinal surface-based morphometry to 874 scans from 440 individuals aged 5-35 years, comparing typical development with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS), a genetic condition characterized by brain dysmaturation, and assessing associations with working memory performance. Our data show a significant age-related volumetric decline that is reduced in 22q11DS left claustra, while surface deformation and thickness analyses revealed spatial patterns unique to hemisphere, group, and developmental age. In controls, the claustrum surface deformed with age in clustered zones along a dorsoventral gradient, and the dorsal-anterior zone thinned across development while the ventral zone thickened. 22q11DS claustra showed less age-related deformation than controls, whose claustrum surface changes associated with verbal working memory. This structural correlate was statistically equivalent to zero in carriers, consistent with a disrupted claustral development to the working memory vulnerability of the syndrome. These findings show the value of surface‑based morphometry over volume alone, highlight dysmaturation and regionally organized claustrum shape variation, and suggest that disrupted structural organization is accompanied by a weaker claustrum-working memory association.

item.title: Naturalistic Movie Viewing Reveals a Distributed Network Supporting Audiovisual Speech Processing
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Traditional paradigms in cognitive neuroscience often fail to capture the richness of real-world experiences. To bridge this gap, researchers increasingly use naturalistic stimuli such as movies, which provide complex, multisensory input. Speech perception is a prime example of such complexity: it is inherently multisensory, involving the integration of auditory cues, lip movements, and facial expressions. Prior studies suggest that the left posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) and superior temporal gyrus (STG) play a critical role in this integration. However, most studies of audiovisual speech have relied on simplified or artificial stimuli, limiting ecological validity. To address these gaps, we analyzed fMRI data from human participants watching two full-length films (500 Days of Summer, Citizenfour) to assess the consistency of multisensory speech processes across distinct genres and narratives. We manually annotated word onset times and modality (audiovisual vs. auditory-only). Across two movies and 38 participants we observed consistent speech-related activation in the pSTS and STG across speech types. Compared to auditory-only speech, audiovisual speech recruited a broad left-lateralized network including the angular gyrus, posterior temporal cortex, temporal pole, and inferior frontal gyrus, along with the right cerebellum. These findings were also consistently present in single-subject data. Importantly, most of the regions observed in our analyses have been implicated in multisensory function in the nonhuman primate literature despite receiving relatively little focus in human neuroimaging. Together our results demonstrate that speech processing during naturalistic viewing recruits a distributed network extending substantially beyond regions traditionally emphasized in audiovisual speech research.

item.title: Brain Dynamics of Persistent Postural-Perceptual Dizziness at Rest Reveal Alterations in Multisensory and Motor Areas
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Persistent Postural-Perceptual Dizziness (PPPD) is a chronic functional disorder with unsteadiness and postural instability, attributed to altered multisensory integration and visual dependence. fMRI studies report altered connectivity in several regions, however, dynamic connectivity remains unexplored. Objectives We characterized resting-state brain dynamics in 17 patients with PPPD and 20 matched healthy controls (HC), and their relationship to clinical and postural measures. Methods Co-Activation Patterns (CAPs) were derived from resting-state fMRI scans for four seeds relevant to multisensory integration, motor output and vestibular processing - right temporo-parietal junction (rTPJ), caudate nucleus, hippocampus and operculo-parietal area 2 (OP2) - and their temporal metrics compared between groups. Partial Least Squares Correlation (PLSC) related CAPs to mood, vertigo, stress, and visual dependence for gait and postural control. Results Patients with PPPD showed altered dynamics seeded from rTPJ (decrease of a salience-coupled CAP, increased entries into a visual/dorsal-attention-coupled CAP), caudate nucleus (increased time in a default mode-coupled CAP, decrease of a salience/visual-coupled CAP) and hippocampus (increase of a default-mode-coupled CAP), but not OP2. PLSC yielded two significant latent components: the first linked rTPJ, OP2 and hippocampal CAPs sharing visual network co-deactivation to stress, mood, vertigo and visual dependence for gait; the second linked all caudate and two rTPJ CAPs to postural sway with eyes closed (visual dependence). Individual brain-behavior scores correlated in both groups. Conclusion Resting-state dynamics are altered in multisensory and motor regions in PPPD, but preserved in OP2, the core vestibular cortex. Brain-behavior organization appears shared across groups, with shifted dynamics in patients.

item.title: Divergence from Diffusion Tensor: a discriminant diffusion marker from single shell MRI
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Purpose: The Divergence from the Diffusion Tensor (DDT) is a new diffusion MRI metric that quantifies how the measured diffusion signal separates from the tensor assumption. It is marker for tissue heterogeneity that is estimated from single-shell data and can be used in brain studies. Methods: There exist other techniques that allow the calculation of how the measured diffusion diverges from the Gaussian and tensor assumptions. However, the calculation requires large data-sets with different b-values, which makes them incompatible which standard diffusion tensor acquisitions. By imposing an initial assumption, an alternative formulation based on one single shell (ie, single b-value) is reported. Results: Publicly available databases are used to test the behavior of DDT against other anisotropy measures. It shows the ability to discriminate different non-Gaussian diffusion scenarios with very low intra-subject variabilities. Conclusions: DDT can extract relevant information from the white matter, without any additional demands on data acquisition and totally compatible with standard diffusion MRI analysis pipelines. This makes DDT a good candidate to be used as an imaging marker for brain studies.

item.title: Impact of Chatbot-Based Cognitive Training on Cognitive Function and White Matter Integrity in Cognitively Unimpaired Older Adults: Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
JMIR aging
Background Cognitive training may enhance cognition and support brain health during aging, but few trials have evaluated readily accessible chatbot-based programs with neuroimaging outcomes. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the effects of a chatbot-based cognitive training program on white matter microstructural organization and cognition in cognitively unimpaired older adults. Methods In a single-blind randomized controlled trial, 72 cognitively unimpaired older adults were assigned to chatbot-based cognitive training (30 min/day, 5 days/week for 12 weeks; n=37) or a no-intervention control (n=35). Diffusion tensor imaging at baseline and 12 weeks quantified fractional anisotropy (FA) in predefined white matter tracts, and cognition was assessed with the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery. Results Groups were comparable at baseline. After 12 weeks, the training group showed significantly less FA reduction than controls in the bilateral tapetum and right posterior thalamic radiation, surviving false discovery rate control (P<.05). The training group also improved on Paired Associates Learning (PAL), an episodic memory measure (P=.04). PAL improvement was positively associated with FA change in the right posterior thalamic radiation and right sagittal stratum (false discovery rate-adjusted P=.04 for each). Conclusions These findings suggest that a 12-week chatbot-based cognitive training program may support episodic memory and the relative maintenance of white matter microstructural organization in selected pathways in cognitively unimpaired older adults, consistent with a brain-maintenance framework. Trial registration CRIS KCT0004630; https://tinyurl.com/4xfesb68.

item.title: Learning from Error Predictions Rather Than Prediction Errors: A Perspective on Self-Supervised Learning in the Brain.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Humans learn by doing and observing but also by imagining the result of simulated actions in their mind. When learning from executed or observed actions, traditional theories posit that behavior improves by minimizing the difference between (1) the perceived outcome derived from sensory feedback and (2) the desired outcome (performance error) or the outcome predicted by an internal model (prediction error, PE). Supporting these theories, decades of electrophysiological studies have documented the role of the dopaminergic system and cerebellum in generating activity patterns compatible with the hypothesized error signals. In comparison, our understanding of the neural basis underlying the ability to learn from simulated actions is far more limited. Here, I argue that this form of self-supervised learning is best described in terms of a quantity known as the predicted performance error (PPE), theorized more than 30 years ago and yet largely overlooked ever since. Complementary to PEs, PPEs reflect "error predictions" between predicted and desired outcomes. Unlike PEs, however, PPEs exist even in the absence of sensory feedback and can in principle serve to evaluate actions without executing them, based on an efference copy of the underlying motor plan. I review evidence supporting the computation of PPEs in the brain and propose a network implementation based on a cortico-basal ganglia loop interacting at multiple timescales with prefrontal, parietal, and hippocampal areas. I then connect PPEs to recent discoveries on motor planning and formulate novel predictions linking PPEs to various high-level brain functions such as metacognition, problem-solving, and deception.

item.title: Normalization Accounts for Temporal Dynamics in the Human Somatosensory Cortex.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Sensory processing is fundamentally shaped by stimulation history. For example, in the visual cortex, neural responses are reduced for repeated or sustained stimuli (adaptation). These phenomena are well characterized and effectively modeled by divisive normalization. We asked whether these same computational principles govern somatosensory processing. We used fMRI (six participants, all female) and intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG, two participants, both male) to measure responses to time-varying vibrotactile stimuli in the human somatosensory cortex. Stimuli consisted of single and paired pulses with durations and interstimulus intervals ranging from 0.05 to 1.2 s. We extracted BOLD time courses to capture neural response amplitudes and high-frequency iEEG broadband envelopes to capture fast neural dynamics. In both experiments, we observed pronounced subadditive temporal summation. Responses to longer or repeated stimuli were consistently lower than predicted by linear integration. Computational modeling revealed that divisive normalization models outperformed linear models in cross-validated accuracy across both datasets. These results demonstrate that somatosensory temporal dynamics closely mirror those in the visual system. Our findings suggest that the nervous system employs similar computational principles across modalities to encode sensory information across time.

item.title: Equidistance between Primary Sensory-Motor Landmarks Shapes Functional Specialization in the Human Brain.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The human cortex is organized around primary sensory-motor landmarks, but the way these distances shape large-scale functional organization remains unclear. Using geodesic measures in males and females, we show that global minimum distance to sensory-motor landmarks aligns with the principal gradient of intrinsic connectivity, reflecting the shift from unimodal to heteromodal cortex, while equidistance between landmarks captures complementary organizational patterns. Heteromodal networks, including default mode, control, and limbic systems, occupy cortical regions that are both distant from primary systems and relatively balanced between them. Subsystems within these networks exhibit distinctive spatial embeddings: core default mode regions sit equidistant between visual and somatomotor cortex, frontotemporal default mode regions favor auditory cortex but remain relatively balanced, and medial temporal regions are biased toward visual cortex. Control network subsystems also vary: the control-DMN subsystem occupies the most distant and equidistant positions, core control is closer to motor regions, and medial control is closer to visual cortex, reflecting their different functional specializations. At the parcel level, greater equidistance predicts stronger task-evoked activation, particularly in heteromodal border zones. These findings highlight two complementary spatial principles-proximity and balance-that structure the cortex, shaping both the location and functional profile of heteromodal networks.

item.title: Individualised electrophysiological neural field models for the assessment of thalamocortical function in disorders of consciousness: A multicentre study.
item.description:
PLoS computational biology
Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying disorders of consciousness (DoC) remains a major challenge, particularly in distinguishing limited awareness in minimally conscious state (MCS) and complete unawareness in unresponsive wakefulness syndrome, also coined vegetative state (UWS/VS). In this multicentre study, we fitted a biophysically informed corticothalamic neural field model to high-density EEG data from two large independent datasets, comprising 203 UWS patients, 270 MCS patients and 74 healthy controls. We then used the fitted parameters to simulate EEG time series on a per-subject basis and compared empirical and simulated complexity metrics. The model reliably captured the spectral features across different states of consciousness and revealed reduced corticothalamic integrity in DoC patients that was more pronounced in UWS than in MCS, supporting the mesocircuit hypothesis. Furthermore, the simulated EEG reproduced the complexity patterns of the empirical recordings, with permutation entropy emerging as a sensitive marker capable of distinguishing between MCS and UWS for both real and simulated time series.

item.title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature.
item.description:
Nature
Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being1 and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits2 , prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person's capacity to regulate emotions3-5 . Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity-trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation-do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits.

item.title: Individualized structural brain network and transcriptomic characterization of heterogeneity in type 2 diabetes mellitus.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a heterogeneous metabolic disorder that also affects the brain, yet prior neuroimaging studies have predominantly focused on group-level comparisons, obscuring interindividual variability in brain structural organization. To capture this heterogeneity, we constructed individualized differential structural covariance networks for 156 individuals with T2DM using 148 healthy controls as a normative reference. Unsupervised clustering based on these individualized networks revealed two neuroanatomical subtypes with distinct network configurations. Most subtype-differentiating edges showed higher values in one subtype, whereas a smaller set of edges, primarily involving the basal ganglia and cerebellum, showed higher values in the other. Integration with transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas identified genes spatially associated with subtype-related differences. These genes were enriched in processes including receptor tyrosine kinase signaling and glycerolipid metabolism, with preferential expression in the striatum and cerebellum. Together, these findings characterize interindividual variation in brain structural covariance in T2DM and identify candidate molecular processes associated with the observed subtype differences.

item.title: Impact of hearing loss on visual selective attention: Evidence from N2pc and resting-state networks.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Efficient visual attention is fundamental to environmental adaptation and social interaction. While previous studies have observed alterations in visual processing among deaf individuals, findings remain controversial regarding whether these changes stem from hearing loss (sensory compensation vs. cognitive deficit) or sign language experience. To address this issue, the present study provides task-related and resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) evidence to disentangle the specific drivers of visual selective attention plasticity. A visual search task was used to examine selective attention in 95 participants (34 prelingual deaf, 27 hearing signers, and 34 hearing nonsigners). Compared to both hearing groups, deaf individuals exhibited significantly lower hit rates and diminished N2-posterior contralateral (N2pc) amplitudes. Hearing signers and nonsigners showed comparable behavioral performance, N2pc amplitudes, and resting-state network topology, whereas the deaf group was further characterized by a degraded resting-state alpha network topology, evidenced by reduced clustering coefficients, global efficiency, and weakened frontal-occipital connectivity. N2pc amplitude correlated significantly with resting-state network properties and behavioral accuracy. These results suggest that deaf individuals may suffer from an imbalance in the regulation of visual selective attention, most clearly indexed by the evoked N2pc and by intrinsic alpha-network organization, and likely linked to increased resource competition following the loss of auditory monitoring. Our findings provide neurophysiological evidence that these attentional deficits are associated with hearing loss rather than with sign-language experience, offering a new perspective for understanding the boundaries of cross-modal plasticity in the human brain.

item.title: Graph Neural Network Reveals the Cortical Morphology of Local Brain Aging in Normal Cognition and Alzheimer's Disease.
item.description:
Neuroinformatics
Estimating brain age (BA) from T1-weighted magnetic resonance images (MRIs) provides a powerful framework for quantifying anatomical brain aging. Whereas global BA (GBA) summarizes overall brain health, local BA (LBA) provides cortically specific patterns of aging at the subject level. Although previous studies have examined anatomical contributors to GBA, to our knowledge, no framework has been established to estimate LBA using cortical morphology. To address this gap, we introduce a graph neural network (GNN) that uses morphometric features-cortical thickness, surface area, curvature, gray/white matter intensity ratio (GWR), sulcal depth-to estimate LBA across the cortical surface at high spatial resolution (mean inter-vertex distance = 1.37 mm). Trained on cortical surface meshes extracted from the MRIs of cognitively normal (CN) adults (N = 14,423), our model achieves better test-retest performance than the existing state-of-the-art, while identifying more biologically plausible patterns of aging in Alzheimer's disease (AD) on the ADNI dataset. Association cortices emerge as primary sites of morphometric aging in CNs, whereas mild cognitive impairment is characterized by widespread aging that is pronounced in the parahippocampal gyrus. AD subjects demonstrate significant aging across the entire cortex, particularly within medial temporal regions and associated cortical networks. Feature ablation highlights curvature and GWR as preferentially sensitive to AD pathology. Regional LBA gaps are significantly associated with neuropsychological measures of AD-related cognitive impairment, linking cortical aging patterns to clinical outcomes. These results demonstrate that GNN-based modeling of cortical morphometry enables biologically interpretable mapping of local brain aging with greater fidelity than prior work.

item.title: Prefrontal Cortical Changes With Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement in Opioid Use Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
JAMA psychiatry
Importance Despite decades of clinical implementation of medications for opioid use disorder (OUD), overdose mortality rates remain high, underscoring a critical need for interventions that target the brain mechanisms underlying addiction. Objective To assess the neural mechanisms of Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE) and their associations with clinical outcomes, including craving and abstinence duration. Design, setting, and participants This randomized clinical trial was conducted from November 2020 to September 2024 among individuals with OUD recruited from an inpatient rehabilitation facility in New York and randomized to MORE or psychoeducational supportive therapy (PST). Data were analyzed from October 2024 to August 2026. Interventions Treatment with MORE (comprising training in mindfulness, drug cue reappraisal, and savoring positive experiences) or PST (active control condition) across 8 weekly 2-hour group sessions. Main outcomes and measures Outcomes included treatment-related changes in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) blood oxygen level-dependent signal (primary), abstinence length (secondary), and cue-induced craving (secondary). Results Drug cue reactivity task analyses included 59 participants (MORE, n = 24; 5 women [20.8%]; mean [SD] age, 43.6 [11.3] years; PST, n = 35; 8 women [22.9%]; mean [SD] age, 42.8 [10.0] years). Movie-watching and follow-up analyses were conducted in subsets of 37 (MORE, n = 18; PST, n = 19) and 38 participants (MORE, n = 13; PST, n = 25), respectively. Compared with PST, MORE reduced drug-biased activity in the middle frontal gyrus and other brain areas, including the precuneus, during downregulation of responses to drug cues relative to upregulation of responses to natural reward cues (even when controlling for passive cue viewing; z > 3.1; P < .05). The shift from drug to natural reward responses in the lateral and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (PFC) was associated with lower cue-induced craving exclusively in the MORE group (z > 3.1; P < .05). Relative to PST, MORE also reduced medial PFC synchronization to naturalistic drug-related movie scenes (q = 0.019) and significantly extended abstinence duration at follow-up (approximately 4 months posttreatment; χ2 = 6.7; P = .04; Cohen w = 0.19). Conclusions and relevance This neuroimaging randomized clinical trial demonstrates that MORE may restructure function in PFC nodes of the reward, salience, and control networks, positioning it as a biologically grounded adjunct to pharmacotherapy for OUD. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04112186.

item.title: Neurotransmitter receptor architecture links local neurochemistry to semantic memory
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
A fundamental challenge in neuroscience is understanding how the molecular and neurochemical architecture of the human cortex gives rise to sophisticated higher cognitive functions. The anterior temporal lobe (ATL) is a key hub for semantic memory, and its underlying GABAergic and glutamatergic neurochemistry supports semantic memory performance. However, the molecular receptor architecture underlying these neurochemical-cognitive relationships remains unknown. Here, we combined imaging transcriptomics and in vivo magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) to investigate how neurotransmitter receptor organisation relates to local neurochemistry and semantic memory in the human ATL. We found that the ATL exhibited a distinct transcriptomically inferred receptor-subunit profile relative to control cortical regions (occipital cortex and vertex). Individual-specific spatial estimates of receptor-subunit gene expression were systematically associated with local GABA+ and Glx concentrations, revealing preferential coupling between GABAergic receptor genes and GABA+ and between glutamatergic receptor genes and Glx, alongside widespread cross-system associations between GABAergic receptor architecture and Glx. ATL GABA+ and Glx concentrations were positively associated with semantic memory performance, and GABAergic and glutamatergic receptor-subunit expression showed selective relationships with semantic memory accuracy. Crucially, mediation analyses revealed that GABA+ mediated associations between GABAergic receptor architecture and semantic performance, whereas Glx mediated both glutamatergic and widespread GABAergic receptor associations. Together, these findings reveal a coupled molecular-neurochemical architecture of the human ATL, linking neurotransmitter receptor organisation to regional neurochemical state and individual differences in semantic memory. Our findings provide a multiscale account of how cortical molecular organisation is associated with human higher cognitive function.

item.title: Microstructure of white matter association tracts in the temporal lobe predicts the timing of electrophysiological activity and behaviour in picture naming
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
White matter (WM) microstructure has been mainly associated with accuracy of picture naming. However, little is known about how WM properties relate to the timing of picture naming and its underlying electrophysiological activity. Here, we linked diffusion-weighted, electrophysiological, and behavioural data, using time-based measures to conceptually connect WM deterioration to alterations in conduction speed and precision. Our sample included individuals of varying age, with or without stroke. We correlated fractional anisotropy (FA) of bilateral WM tracts traversing the temporal lobe with mean response times (RTs) and response time variability (coefficient of variation, CV) in picture naming, and with the onset latency of neuronal activity, represented by the electrophysiological P2 component time-locked to picture onset. We selected tracts showing associations with P2 latency and naming performance separately, on which we conducted path analyses examining the relationship between structure, neuronal activity and behaviour. Depending on the tract, higher FA was associated with faster and/or more consistent naming, suggesting that ventral tracts differentially contribute to naming speed and consistency. Importantly, path modelling for the right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF) revealed that FA predicted P2 latency, which in turn predicted RTs, possibly reflecting a structure-activity-behaviour relationship in lexical-semantic processing. P2 source reconstruction demonstrated anatomical proximity to posterior segments of the right IFOF, supporting these findings. Overall, this study provides a proof of concept for modelling structure-activity-behaviour relationships in language research, while highlighting the need for elaboration of such relations at a more mechanistic level.

item.title: Older Adults Show Preserved Neural Signatures of Audiovisual Integration but Altered Links to Speech Comprehension
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Older adults often experience difficulty understanding speech in noisy environments despite relatively preserved hearing. Although visual speech cues can improve speech perception, it remains unclear whether the neural mechanisms supporting audiovisual integration are preserved in healthy ageing. We addressed this question using magnetoencephalography (MEG) combined with Rapid Invisible Frequency Tagging (RIFT) during challenging audiovisual speech task. Forty younger and forty older adults attended to one of two competing speech streams while the speaker’s lip movements were frequency tagged, with the visual modulation driven by either the attended or unattended speech envelope. Task-Relevant amplitude modulation of frequency tagging in visual speech improved speech comprehension in younger adults as previously reported for this cohort; this accuracy benefit was absent in older adults. Auditory and visual tagging responses were modulated by task relevance similarly across age groups, indicating largely preserved modality-specific sensory processing in older adults. Intermodulation responses, reflecting nonlinear interactions between auditory and visual speech signals, also remained sensitive to task relevance and did not differ in their condition-dependent modulation between age groups. Greater Task-Relevant versus Task-Irrelevant differences in intermodulation coherence were also associated with greater comprehension benefits in younger adults; no significant association was found in older adults, and this relationship differed significantly between age groups. These findings suggest that the absence of a comprehension benefit in older adults is linked to a change in the relationship between audiovisual intermodulation and behaviour, despite largely preserved task-sensitive brain responses.
